titulo.texto: The Causeway of the Twenty-One Altars

frase_gancho.texto: A row of altars that looks like a calendar laid out on the ground.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue along your route: what comes next shows how people lived and worked in the city.

guion_corto.texto: A causeway is a wide, raised road. This one has twenty-one altars along its sides. According to the INAH, they represent the months of the ceremonial year and, in one case, days. México Desconocido describes twenty round altars and one square one, and suggests that they were used to count the 260-day calendar. Count them as you go. Both accounts agree that the altars had to do with the calendar. Walking among them was a way of moving through that calendar step by step. This is a proposal by specialists, not a settled fact, and that is why it is worth seeing them with your own eyes. Here, time was not only watched. It was walked.

guion_largo.texto:
Count with your eyes. Along this causeway there is a row of altars, twenty-one in all, according to the INAH.

A causeway is a wide, raised road, made for walking in an orderly way. This one is part of the middle level of the city, and the altars line up along its sides.

The INAH explains that they represent the months of the ceremonial year and that, in one case, they represent days. In other words, each altar has a place within a calendar.

México Desconocido gives more detail. It speaks of twenty round altars and one square one, in the sector it calls La Malinche, and says that they may have been used to calculate the 260-day calendar. That ritual calendar was used throughout Mesoamerica.

How they were used is what specialists propose, but it is not a settled fact. What we do know is that their number and their arrangement in a row invite us to think of counts and cycles.

Perhaps people walked the causeway in a ceremony, stopping at each altar. This is a possibility, not a proven fact.

If you walk among them, do it slowly. Each step brings you closer to the next altar and reminds you that in Xochicalco time had a shape and a place, and could be stepped on.

The city did not only measure time by watching the sky. It also measured it with stones set in the ground.

texto.Quantity: twenty-one altars, according to the INAH
texto.Shapes: twenty round and one square, according to México Desconocido

texto.pregunta: Myth: We know exactly how the altars were used.
texto.respuesta: Reality: No. Specialists propose that they represent months and days of the calendar, but there is no text that explains their use.
